createOrReplace.title: ERP Implementation in 2026: Why 70% Fall Short
createOrReplace.html:
ERP implementation still disappoints more often than it delivers: Gartner says 70% of ERP initiatives fail to fully meet their original business goals, and 25% fail catastrophically. The causes are rarely the software. They are unclear scope, heavy customisation, weak testing and late change management, all of which an Indian mid-market firm can control before it signs a contract.

This matters now because Indian companies are buying ERP faster than ever. IMARC Group puts the India ERP market at $1,929.8 million in 2025 and expects $3,651.9 million by 2034. GST, e-invoicing and cloud pricing are pulling SMEs off Tally sheets and spreadsheets. More projects means more failed projects, unless buyers learn from the benchmarks below.

TL;DR

  • Gartner: 70% of ERP initiatives miss their original goals; 25% fail catastrophically.
  • Panorama Consulting: only 55% of ERP projects finish within budget and 58% on time.
  • McKinsey and Oxford found large IT programmes run 45% over budget and deliver 56% less value.
  • The median ERP project cost $450,000 in Panorama's 2025 study, and 72% of buyers preferred SaaS.
  • In India, 71.48% of new ERP licences in 2025 were cloud, per Mordor Intelligence.

What is the real ERP failure rate in 2026?

Roughly seven in ten ERP projects fall short of what they promised, and about one in four fails outright. That is the consistent finding across Gartner, Panorama and Argon & Co research.

At its November 2025 Symposium, Gartner reported that 70% of ERP initiatives fail to fully meet their original business use-case goals, according to The Register's coverage. Gartner's research page goes further: by 2027, it predicts more than 70% of recently implemented ERP initiatives will not fully meet their original business goals. Argon & Co's 2026 whitepaper reached a similar conclusion, finding that fewer than half of ERP programmes achieve or exceed their intended outcomes.

"Failure" here rarely means the system never goes live. It means the business case erodes: the go-live slips, the budget grows, and the promised savings arrive late or partially. A 2023 survey of 251 tech leaders, cited by The Register, found 73% said their ERP strategy was not strongly aligned with their business strategy. That misalignment is where most of the value leaks.

How often do ERP projects go over budget and over time?

About a third of ERP projects run over budget and a similar share run late. Panorama's surveys put the on-budget rate at just over half.

Panorama Consulting's study of 131 organisations (polled between August 2022 and December 2023) found 55% completed their projects within budget and 58% on time, as reported by Accounting Today. On the other side, 32.8% finished slightly or significantly over budget and 31.3% finished later than planned. Panorama's 2026 ERP Report shows little change: 30% of respondents said their ERP projects were over budget, according to TechTarget.

Large programmes are worse. A McKinsey and University of Oxford study, cited in Argon & Co's 2026 report, found large IT programmes run 45% over budget on average and deliver 56% less value than planned. The public examples are stark. The Register reports Birmingham City Council's Oracle ERP grew from around £19 million to £170 million in total project costs. Zimmer Biomet filed a $172 million claim against its implementation partner after a 2024 launch, per Consultancy-me.

Why do ERP implementations fail?

ERP implementations fail mainly because of business misalignment, uncontrolled customisation, thin testing and late change management, not because the software is wrong.

Argon & Co's 2026 report singles out inadequate testing as a recurring cause of derailed ERP transformations. Testing is usually the phase that gets squeezed when design runs late. The same report notes that 89% of organisations are now piloting or using AI-enabled quality engineering tools, per Capgemini's World Quality Report 2026, so automated regression testing is no longer exotic.

Customisation is the second trap. Mordor Intelligence reports that customisation adds 40% to ERP cost in India, and every custom object becomes something to re-test at each upgrade. The third is strategy: when 73% of tech leaders say their ERP plan is not aligned with business strategy, scope decisions get made by whoever shouts loudest during workshops.

How much does an ERP implementation cost, and how long does it take?

Panorama's 2025 study found a median ERP project cost of $450,000 and a typical deployment of nine months, down from 15.5 months a year earlier.

That sample of 172 companies was mostly large multinationals, so Indian mid-market budgets will usually be lower in absolute terms. The ratios still travel. In the same report, 8% of projects had significant budget overruns and 24% ran slightly over budget, according to iStart. Faster deployment tracks the move to SaaS: 72% of respondents preferred SaaS over hosted or managed options.

Inside India, geography matters. Mordor Intelligence cites Deloitte data showing Tier-II city roll-outs take 14.6 months against 9.2 months in metros, largely because of thinner consultant benches and slower data clean-up. Plan your ERP implementation cost and timeline around where your plants and warehouses actually are, not where the vendor's project office sits.

Is ERP still worth it for Indian businesses?

Yes, when it is scoped tightly. Most firms that finish an ERP implementation report clear productivity and cost gains.

In Panorama's 2025 data, 82% of organisations reported higher productivity and efficiency after go-live, 70% reported lower operating or labour costs, and 65% reported better customer experience. AI is also arriving inside ERP: the share deploying AI significantly or moderately rose from 53% to 73% in a year, per iStart.

Globally, the market keeps growing. Fortune Business Insights valued ERP software at $92.6 billion in 2025 and forecasts $281.6 billion by 2034, a 13% compound annual growth rate, as reported by TechTarget. India's market is growing at 7.12% a year to 2034, per IMARC Group, with SMEs the fastest-growing segment at 19.2% annual growth through 2031, according to Mordor Intelligence.

What does the Indian ERP market look like?

India's ERP market is cloud-first, manufacturing-heavy and dominated by five vendors, with a long tail of SMEs still on manual books.

Mordor Intelligence's 2026 report gives the shape of it. Cloud took 71.48% of new ERP licences in 2025. Manufacturing accounted for 31.23% of ERP spending. SAP, Oracle, Microsoft, Infor and Ramco together hold 59% of the market. Yet 78% of Tier-II and Tier-III manufacturers still use manual ledgers, and a SIDBI survey cited in the report found 48% of SMEs name cost as their main barrier.

How to de-risk your ERP implementation: a 7-step checklist

  1. Write the business case first. Name three to five measurable outcomes (days to close, inventory turns, order-to-cash time) before talking to vendors.
  2. Map processes as they are. Document today's workflows, including the Excel and WhatsApp workarounds. Those are your real requirements.
  3. Adopt standard processes by default. Treat every customisation as a cost line that needs a business owner and a reason.
  4. Clean data before migration. Item masters, vendor masters and open balances cause more go-live delays than code.
  5. Budget for testing. Protect integration and user-acceptance testing time; automate regression tests for GST, e-invoicing and e-way bill flows.
  6. Start change management at kickoff. Name process owners on the shop floor and in finance, not only in IT.
  7. Integrate, don't bend. Where a workflow is truly unique, build a small app on top of the ERP through its APIs instead of modifying the core.

What this means for Indian businesses

For an Indian manufacturer, distributor or hospital group, the lesson from the data is narrow scope and clean edges. Buy a standard cloud ERP for finance, inventory and compliance. Keep the core close to vanilla. Build the parts that actually differentiate you, such as a dealer portal, a production scheduler or a WhatsApp approval flow, as separate software that talks to the ERP. From the way we build, that split keeps upgrades cheap and lets each piece ship in weeks rather than quarters.

Frequently asked questions

What percentage of ERP implementations fail?

Gartner reports that 70% of ERP initiatives fail to fully meet their original business goals and 25% fail catastrophically. Panorama Consulting's surveys show about a third of projects run over budget or late. Most "failures" are partial: the system goes live, but costs rise and benefits arrive later than the business case assumed.

How long does an ERP implementation take?

Panorama Consulting's 2025 study found a typical deployment of nine months, down from 15.5 months the year before, helped by SaaS adoption. In India, Deloitte data cited by Mordor Intelligence shows Tier-II roll-outs take 14.6 months against 9.2 months in metro cities, so location and consultant availability matter.

What is the biggest driver of ERP implementation cost overruns?

Customisation and scope creep are the biggest controllable drivers. Mordor Intelligence reports that customisation adds 40% to ERP cost in India. Poor data quality and squeezed testing add rework late in the project, when changes are most expensive. A fixed scope and a standard-first design policy reduce both.

Is cloud ERP better than on-premise for Indian SMEs?

For most SMEs, yes. Cloud took 71.48% of new ERP licences in India in 2025, according to Mordor Intelligence, and Panorama found 72% of buyers prefer SaaS. Cloud ERP lowers upfront cost, ships GST and e-invoicing updates centrally, and usually deploys faster than on-premise installations.

Should we customise our ERP or build separate software?

Keep the ERP core standard and build unique workflows as separate applications connected through APIs. Heavy core customisation must be re-tested at every upgrade. A small custom app for a dealer portal or production planning can change quickly without touching finance and compliance logic inside the ERP.
